666.title: Hanukkah: the oil (Shabbat 21b)
666.hook: the Talmud's story of one jar of oil lasting eight days
666.howItsDone: Many Jews light Hanukkah lamps with olive oil to recall the jar in the Talmud's story, and eat foods fried in oil, like latkes and sufganiyot, during the eight nights.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Maccabees, and a new altar dedicated for eight days. Your line was the few against the many. Did you stand for your one small thing? Today, the same eight days, told a very different way. Day six hundred sixty-six.

One little jar of oil, enough for one night, and it burned for eight. That's the Hanukkah of greeting cards and children's books. It's why people eat foods fried in oil. But yesterday's story, from First Maccabees, doesn't mention oil at all. So where does the jar come from? The telling everyone repeats is on a page of the Talmud, in the middle of a long discussion about which wicks and oils you may use for Shabbat candles. And it starts with a question that sounds almost naive.
screen: `EVERYONE KNOWS THE OIL.` → `FIRST MACCABEES DOESN'T SAY IT.` → `ONE PAGE OF THE TALMUD.`

segments.voice: The question, in tractate Shabbat, page 21b, is simply: what is Hanukkah? As if the rabbis are asking, why do we keep this at all? And the answer is a short story. When the Greeks entered the Temple, they made all the oils impure. When the Hasmonean family, the Maccabees, defeated them, they searched and found just one jar of oil still sealed with the high priest's seal. It held enough to light the lamp for a single day. A miracle happened, and they lit from it for eight days. The next year, the story ends, they set those days as festival days, for praise and thanksgiving. That's the whole account: a few lines. Notice what it leaves out. No battles, no Judah, no Antiochus. Readers have offered different explanations for why the rabbis told it this way. Some suggest that after later revolts against Rome ended in disaster, the rabbis preferred to stress God's quiet help over victory in battle. Others point out that the Talmud seems to assume its readers know the history, and only adds what's missing. Either way, the story on the greeting cards is this one: not a war, but a lamp. And its point is small and stubborn. A sealed jar, one day's worth, nowhere near enough. They lit it anyway. That's the miracle the rabbis chose to remember: not that there was plenty, but that the little they had was enough to begin.
screen: `WHAT IS HANUKKAH?` · `ONE JAR, THE HIGH PRIEST'S SEAL.` · `ONE DAY'S OIL, EIGHT DAYS' LIGHT.` · `A LAMP, NOT A WAR.` · then, large: `A LITTLE LASTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: make a little go far. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you have only a little of right now: time, patience, money, energy, hope. Instead of waiting until there's enough, picture using that little bit, on purpose, today. One kind word with the patience you have left. Ten minutes with the time you have. Light it anyway. Breathe slowly, as if you're watching a small flame hold. The bell holds the time.
Hanukkah. The dedication, and in the Talmud's telling, the eight days one jar of oil kept burning. Today's word.
Your line: a little lasts. Today, spend the small amount you have of something good, instead of saving it for when there's more. Day six hundred sixty-six.

667.title: Hanukkah: show the light
667.hook: the lights go where passers-by can see
667.howItsDone: Families light the Hanukkah menorah at nightfall, adding one light each night, and place it by the door or in a window facing the street so passers-by can see; many communities also hold public menorah lightings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hanukkah's jar of oil, one day's worth, burning for eight. Your line was a little lasts. Did you spend a little of something good? Today, where the light goes once it's lit. Day six hundred sixty-seven.

An early winter evening, a street of houses and apartments. In one window, a row of small flames. In another, a little glass box by the front door, with oil lamps inside. On an apartment balcony, electric bulbs. Plenty of what happens in a Jewish home stays inside, among family. These lights are different. They're placed so that someone walking past, someone who may not know or care what they mean, can see them. And there's a rule behind that, with a two-word name.
screen: `FLAMES IN THE WINDOWS.` → `A GLASS BOX BY THE DOOR.` → `FOR SOMEONE WALKING PAST.`

segments.voice: Pirsumei nisa is Aramaic. It means publicizing the miracle. It sits behind many of the rules about where and when the Hanukkah lights are lit. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, says the lamp should be set at the entrance of the house, on the outside. If you live upstairs, you place it in a window facing the public street. Its time, the Talmud says, is from when the sun goes down until the last people have gone home from the market, because that's when the street is full of people to see it. There's even a rule that you may not use the Hanukkah light for anything practical, like reading. That's one reason for the extra candle, the shammash, the helper: you use that one, and the others are just for showing. Then comes a striking line. In a time of danger, the Talmud says, it's enough to set the lamp on your table inside. Showing the light matters, but not more than a life. Families in dangerous times and places have done exactly that, lighting quietly, indoors. And in safer times and places, the lights came back out to the windows, and in some cities, to giant public lamps in town squares. The principle is the same in every case: a miracle that stays private isn't finished being told. The lights are meant to be noticed, and the person who notices them doesn't have to be Jewish, or even curious. They just have to walk by.
screen: `PUBLICIZING THE MIRACLE.` · `AT THE DOOR, FACING THE STREET.` · `UNTIL THE MARKET EMPTIES.` · `IN DANGER, THE TABLE IS ENOUGH.` · then, large: `SHOW THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share one piece of good news. Breathe, and look back over the last week. Find one good thing: a kindness someone did for you, a worry that turned out fine, a small win. Good news has a way of staying indoors, unspoken, while bad news gets told five times. Choose who might like to hear this one. Picture telling them. Then sit with the good thing itself, quietly, like a flame in a window. The bell holds the time.
Pirsumei nisa. Publicizing the miracle: the reason the Hanukkah lights face the street. Today's word.
Your line: show the light. Today, tell one person one piece of good news you'd normally keep to yourself. Day six hundred sixty-seven.

668.title: Hanukkah: Maoz Tzur
668.hook: a medieval song sung after lighting, recalling many rescues
668.howItsDone: In many Ashkenazi homes, the family sings Maoz Tzur together after lighting the Hanukkah candles each night, usually the first verse; Sephardi and Mizrahi families often sing other hymns or Psalm 30.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pirsumei nisa, the lights placed where passers-by can see. Your line was show the light. Did you tell someone your good news? Today, what people sing once the lights are lit. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

The candles are lit. The blessings are said. Kids are already eyeing the doughnuts. And then, in many homes, before anyone moves, someone starts a song. Plenty of people know the tune who don't know most of the words; they hum through the middle and come back loud for the end. Many families sing only the first verse. But it has six, and if you read them all, you find it isn't only a song about Hanukkah. It's a song about a lot of nights like this one.
screen: `THE CANDLES ARE LIT.` → `EVERYONE KNOWS THE TUNE.` → `SIX VERSES, NOT ONE.`

segments.voice: The song is called Maoz Tzur. Maoz means stronghold, a fortress. Tzur means rock. The Torah uses rock as a name for God; in the old Jewish translation, Moses sings, "The Rock, His work is perfect." So the song opens by calling God the fortress-rock of my salvation. Who wrote it? The poet signed it in a way medieval Hebrew poets liked: the first letters of the first five verses spell a name, Mordechai. Nobody knows for certain who this Mordechai was. Now the verses. The first looks forward to a rebuilt Temple. The second remembers slavery in Egypt, and the way out. The third, the exile to Babylon, and the return after seventy years. The fourth, Haman, who wanted to destroy the Jews of Persia, and the story we'll meet at Purim. Only the fifth gets to the Greeks, the Hasmoneans, and the jar of oil. And the sixth, likely added later, asks for one more rescue, in the poet's own time. So Hanukkah, in this song, is one link in a chain. Danger, then rescue. Danger, then rescue. People sang it in places where the danger was not ancient history. The English version some families sing, Rock of Ages, is a loose adaptation rather than a translation. And Sephardi and Mizrahi families often sing other songs, or other tunes. The words that travel everywhere are the first two: fortress, rock.
screen: `MAOZ: FORTRESS. TZUR: ROCK.` · `SIGNED BY A POET, MORDECHAI.` · `EGYPT, BABYLON, HAMAN, GREECE.` · `ONE LINK IN A CHAIN.` · then, large: `ROCK OF AGES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sing one song of rescue. Before the bell, think of a song that has carried you through something: a hard year, a long drive, a loss. It doesn't have to be religious. Hum the first line, quietly, or just hear it in your head. Then think of one rescue in your own story, a time you got through. Let the song and the memory sit together. Breathe with them. The bell holds the time.
Hanukkah. Dedication, and in Maoz Tzur, one rescue in a long chain of rescues, sung after the lights. Today's word.
Your line: rock of ages. Today, when something feels shaky, hum your song of rescue and remember one time you got through. Day six hundred sixty-eight.

669.title: The Tenth of Tevet
669.hook: a fast for the siege of Jerusalem, now also a day of Kaddish for those whose death date is unknown
669.tomorrow: Tu BiShvat: a seder of fruits
669.howItsDone: On the Tenth of Tevet, observant Jews fast from dawn until nightfall and add Selichot prayers; in many communities, especially in Israel, Kaddish is said and candles lit for Holocaust victims whose date of death is unknown.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maoz Tzur, the song of many rescues. Your line was rock of ages. Did you hum your song of rescue? Today, a short winter fast, about one of the times the rescue didn't come. Day six hundred sixty-nine.

Many Jewish families keep a yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death. A candle burns for a day, a son or daughter says Kaddish in the synagogue, someone tells a story about the person at dinner. It's a date that holds a life. But what if you don't have the date? What if a whole branch of your family tree simply stops, in a town that no longer exists, in a year you can only guess, and nobody survived to say which day? For millions of Jewish families after the Holocaust, that was not a hypothetical. And the answer they were given was a fast day that already existed, two and a half thousand years old.
screen: `A DATE THAT HOLDS A LIFE.` → `WHAT IF THERE IS NO DATE?` → `AN OLD FAST, A NEW TASK.`

segments.voice: The Tenth of Tevet remembers where the destruction of Jerusalem began. The book of Kings gives the date. In the old Jewish translation: "in the tenth month, in the tenth day of the month," Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, came against Jerusalem with his whole army, and laid siege to it. That siege ended, about a year and a half later, with the city broken and the Temple burned. The prophet Zechariah already names the fasts that grew up around these losses, among them, "the fast of the tenth." And he adds a promise: they will one day become times of joy and gladness. So the day began as the start of a catastrophe, not the catastrophe itself. People fast from dawn until nightfall, and add special prayers of repentance. It's one of the shorter fasts; the night before is not included. Then, in the years after the Holocaust, Israel's Chief Rabbinate gave the day a second purpose. It became the general day of Kaddish: a day for saying the mourner's prayer for those whose date of death is unknown. Many of the six million have no known yahrzeit. On the Tenth of Tevet, their children and grandchildren, and people with no known connection to them at all, say Kaddish for them, and light candles. Holocaust Remembrance Day, which we'll meet in the spring, is the date most people know. But for many communities, this older fast carries the same names. A siege that began the losses, and a day that gives a date to the dead who never got one.
screen: `THE TENTH MONTH, THE TENTH DAY.` · `THE SIEGE OF JERUSALEM BEGINS.` · `ZECHARIAH: THE FAST OF THE TENTH.` · `A KADDISH FOR UNKNOWN DATES.` · then, large: `FOR THE UNKNOWN DATES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone with no known date. Breathe slowly. Think of someone whose story you only partly know: a great-grandparent, a name in an old photo, a person you've read about whose ending nobody recorded. You may not know their face. Just hold the fact that they lived, and that they were someone's child. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If not, simply sit with them, in silence. The bell holds the time.
The Tenth of Tevet. The fast for the start of the siege of Jerusalem, and the general day of Kaddish for those with no known date. Today's word.
Your line: for the unknown dates. Today, ask someone in your family one question about a person in your past whose story is fading. Write down the answer. Day six hundred sixty-nine.

670.title: Tu BiShvat: a seder of fruits
670.hook: the Safed mystics made a seder of fruits and four cups of wine
670.howItsDone: Many Jews eat fruits of the Land of Israel on Tu BiShvat, especially the seven species, and some hold a Tu BiShvat seder following the kabbalists' order of fruits and four cups of wine moving from white to red.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Tenth of Tevet, the siege and the general day of Kaddish. Your line was for the unknown dates. Did you ask about someone whose story is fading? Today, a month later, the trees. Day six hundred seventy.

It begins as a line in a tax code. The Mishnah lists four new years in the Jewish calendar, and one of them is for trees. Why do trees need a new year? Because the Torah's tithes and fruit laws count a tree's age, and someone has to decide when a tree's year turns over. The schools of Shammai and Hillel disagreed about the date, and Hillel's view won: the fifteenth of the month of Shevat. In Hebrew numbers, fifteen is written tet-vav, said tu. Tu BiShvat. For a long time, that was mostly it: a date for bookkeeping. Then a group of mystics sat down at a table and turned it into a feast.
screen: `FOUR NEW YEARS.` → `ONE IS FOR TREES.` → `FROM BOOKKEEPING TO A FEAST.`

segments.voice: The mystics were kabbalists in the tradition of Safed, the hill town in the Galilee where a circle of Jewish mystics gathered. Their followers wrote a little book, later printed under the name Pri Etz Hadar, fruit of the goodly tree. It lays out a Tu BiShvat seder, an ordered meal, like Passover's, but made of fruit. First, the fruits of the Land of Israel. The Torah praises the land, in the old Jewish translation, as "a land of wheat and barley, and vines and fig-trees and pomegranates; a land of olive-trees and honey." The rabbis read that honey as date honey. Seven species, and the seder makes sure to eat them. Then the fruits are sorted in three groups. Ones with a hard shell outside, like walnuts and pomegranates. Ones with a hard pit inside, like olives and dates. And ones you can eat completely, like figs and grapes. For the mystics, these stood for layers of the world, from the most guarded to the most open. And then the four cups of wine. The first is white. The second is white with a little red. The third, mostly red. The fourth, all red. Some read it as winter warming into spring, color slowly coming into the land. A blessing is said over each new fruit, and passages from the Bible and the Zohar are read between them. Today, families, schools and environmental groups hold Tu BiShvat seders, some traditional, some new. At the heart of the old order is a simple act: paying attention to what grows on a tree, and saying a blessing before eating it.
screen: `THE MYSTICS OF SAFED.` · `THE SEVEN SPECIES.` · `SHELL, PIT, OR OPEN.` · `FOUR CUPS, WHITE TO RED.` · then, large: `FRUITS OF THE TREE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat three kinds of fruit. If you have them nearby, set out three: maybe one with a peel, one with a pit, one you can eat whole. If you don't, picture them. Before the bell, hold one, and look at it properly: its color, its weight, the tree it came from, the hands that picked it. If you say blessings, this is a moment for one. Then eat slowly, one at a time, noticing how each is different. The bell holds the time.
Tu BiShvat. The fifteenth of Shevat, the new year for trees, and for the mystics, a seder of fruits and four cups. Today's word.
Your line: fruits of the tree. Today, before you eat one piece of fruit, stop and think of the tree it grew on. Day six hundred seventy.

671.title: Tu BiShvat: planting
671.hook: many plant trees or give to planting on this day
671.howItsDone: Many Jews plant trees on Tu BiShvat, especially in Israel, where schools hold planting days; elsewhere many give to tree-planting funds, eat fruits of the land, or care for plants at home.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the mystics' Tu BiShvat seder, with its fruits and four cups. Your line was fruits of the tree. Did you stop to think of the tree? Today, the other half of the day: putting one in the ground. Day six hundred seventy-one.

A man is walking along a road and sees someone planting a carob tree. He stops and asks: how long until this tree bears fruit? Seventy years, comes the answer. The traveler looks him up and down. And you're sure you'll be alive in seventy years to eat from it? The planter keeps digging. That's a story from the Talmud, in tractate Taanit. The traveler is Choni, whom the same page of the Talmud remembers for praying down rain, and his story goes on to become something like Rip Van Winkle. But the planter's answer is the part people quote.
screen: `A MAN PLANTS A CAROB.` → `SEVENTY YEARS TO FRUIT.` → `WILL YOU BE ALIVE TO EAT IT?`

segments.voice: The planter says, roughly: I found this world full of carob trees. My ancestors planted them for me, so I'm planting for my children. Then Choni sits down to eat, falls asleep, and sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, he sees a man gathering carobs from that very tree. Are you the one who planted it? No, the man says: my grandfather did. That's the Talmud's picture of planting. You do it for someone you may never meet. The midrash finds the same idea in the Torah's command, when Israel enters the land, to plant fruit trees. Even God, it notes, began the world by planting: Genesis says God planted a garden in Eden. So planting becomes a way of imitating God. Another teaching, from a collection called Avot of Rabbi Natan, is even bolder. It's attributed to Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai: if you're holding a sapling in your hand, and someone tells you the Messiah has arrived, plant the sapling first. Then go out to greet him. Tu BiShvat became a planting day only in modern times. The story usually told is that a teacher in the village of Zikhron Yaakov took his students out to plant trees on the fifteenth of Shevat, and the custom spread through schools and, later, tree-planting campaigns. Today, some people plant on this day, and others give money for planting. In the northern winter it's often too cold to dig, so people plant indoors, or give, or water what's already growing. The point is the same as the carob tree. Somebody planted for you.
screen: `MY ANCESTORS PLANTED FOR ME.` · `CHONI SLEEPS SEVENTY YEARS.` · `GOD PLANTED A GARDEN FIRST.` · `PLANT THE SAPLING, THEN GO.` · then, large: `PLANT SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: water a plant. If there's one near you, a houseplant, a window box, a tree outside, give it water now, slowly, and watch the soil drink. If there isn't, picture a tree you've loved, and the person who might have planted it. Then sit, breathe, and think of one person who planted something for you: a lesson, a habit, a kindness you're still eating from. The bell holds the time.
Tu BiShvat. The new year for trees, and in modern times, a day for planting what others will enjoy. Today's word.
Your line: plant something. Today, start one small thing whose fruit someone else will probably enjoy more than you. Day six hundred seventy-one.

672.title: The Fast of Esther (Esther 4:16)
672.hook: a fast the day before Purim, for Esther's three days of fasting
672.howItsDone: On the Fast of Esther, the thirteenth of Adar, observant Jews fast from dawn until nightfall, often give charity in the afternoon in memory of the half-shekel, and break the fast after hearing the Megillah read on Purim night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tu BiShvat's planting, and Choni's carob tree. Your line was plant something. Did you start something someone else will enjoy? Today we move to late winter, and the road to Purim. Day six hundred seventy-two.

A young woman is standing outside a door. Behind it sits the king of Persia, who also happens to be her husband. There's a law: anyone who walks into the king's inner court without being called is put to death, unless the king holds out his golden scepter. She hasn't been called in thirty days. And her people, the Jews of the Persian empire, have a date set for their destruction. Her cousin Mordecai has just told her that if she stays silent, she may not escape either. She doesn't go in yet. First, she sends back a message.
screen: `A DOOR SHE CAN'T WALK THROUGH.` → `NOT CALLED IN THIRTY DAYS.` → `FIRST, A MESSAGE.`

segments.voice: Esther's message is in chapter four. She asks Mordecai to gather all the Jews of Shushan and fast for her: no food, no drink, for three days, night and day. She and her maids will fast too. Then she'll go in to the king, against the law. And her last words, in the old Jewish translation: "and if I perish, I perish." The line is very quiet. No speech about courage. Just a decision, and a fast to get ready for it. Now, the Fast of Esther as people keep it today falls on the thirteenth of Adar, the day before Purim. But the book never dates Esther's own three-day fast, and its timeline leads tradition to place it in the spring month of Nisan, almost a year earlier. So why the thirteenth of Adar? The thirteenth was the day set for the attack, and the day the Jews had to defend themselves. Later authorities explain that people fasted and prayed on that day of battle, as they had with Esther. The book itself, near its end, mentions fasts and cries as part of what the Jews took on. The fast is first described as a custom after the Talmud's time, and it's one of the minor fasts: dawn to nightfall. If Purim falls on a Sunday, the fast moves back to Thursday, so it doesn't land on Shabbat. In the afternoon, there's a custom of giving coins to charity, recalling the half-shekel. And at nightfall, the fast breaks straight into Purim: the scroll is read, and the feast begins. Hunger first. Then joy.
